Hi Cassandra —

Thanks for the clear questions. Below is a concise breakdown you can paste into your assessment. I'm also attaching a simple matrix (redwood-data-hold-matrix.xlsx) that maps triggers to behaviors.

Summary (default behavior):
- Requests (raw request body including text prompts and non-sensitive metadata): stored by default for 45 days in hosted plans, unless customer opts into ephemeral mode. Requests are treated as primary artifacts and will be frozen on legal hold.
- Outputs (model-generated text, attachments produced by tool calls): stored by default for 90 days. Final outputs are considered secondary artifacts; they are frozen if an active legal hold exists for the session or account.
- Streaming tokens: streaming buffers are transient by default and only materialize into stored outputs if the request completes successfully and the final output is generated. The transient streaming window is not subject to default retention unless captured as an output.
- Derivatives (embeddings, reranking scores, cached KV snapshots): considered derived artifacts. By default, embeddings are retained for 180 days to support embedding index performance; KV cache entries are ephemeral (TTL tied to active session, typically 24–72 hours) unless explicitly persisted by the customer.

Hold & erase flow (default):
1) Capture: request accepted -> request+metadata logged (45d) -> outputs saved if generation completes (90d) -> derivatives created per configuration (embeddings 180d).
2) Hold: legal/legal-hold flag freezes associated primary and secondary artifacts immediately (requests, outputs, derivatives tied to hold id). Hold does not cancel encryption or key rotation; artifacts remain encrypted and retained until hold cleared.
3) Erase: once hold cleared, artifacts revert to normal TTLs and will be scheduled for deletion per the standard purge window. Deletions are irreversible; audit entries are kept in the control-plane audit log (access-only) for 365 days.

Notes & exceptions:
- Dedicated/Private deployments: default retention windows are configurable via account settings and may be extended by contract.
- Customer-managed retention: we support explicit TTLs and an API to request immediate purge (subject to hold checks).
- Regulatory exports and backups: snapshots for disaster recovery are encrypted and retained per our backup schedule; we provide a documented purge path on request.

I'll loop in Karthik below to add any technical nuances on KV and streaming artifacts. Let me know if you want this reworded into a single-paragraph vendor-ready blurb.

Cheers,
Kimberly Park
Head of Sales, Enterprise
Redwood Inference

Hi Cassandra — quick technical clarifications from infra: 

- Streaming tokens: the runtime maintains an in-memory buffer for open streams; we only write to persistent storage when a generation commit is performed. If you call the commit API, that output is treated like a normal "output" artifact and inherits the 90d TTL. If you never commit, nothing is persisted beyond the ephemeral buffer (and it's not searchable).

- KV cache: the serving runtime's KV cache is used for performance and is not part of the observability logs. We do not persist per-session KV snapshots to long-term storage unless the customer uses our "persist-kv" option; default TTL is 48 hours after last activity.

- Embeddings lifecycle: embedding vectors created by the Redwood Optimize pipeline are stored in a managed index. By default the index keeps vectors for 180d, after which vectors are swept unless the customer pins them or has their own index retention policy. We expose APIs for bulk purge and per-vector delete.

- Audit trail: control-plane audit logs capture erase and hold operations (who requested, timestamp, scope) and are immutable for 365d for incident forensics.

If you want, we can provide an exportable JSON snippet that maps each artifact to default TTLs and hold behavior.

—Karthik
Principal Infra Engineer

Hi Cassandra —

Answers inline: 
1) Ephemeral accounts: if an account is set to ephemeral-by-default, outputs are not persisted into regular backup snapshots. Disaster-recovery snapshots still exist for platform resilience, but they are encrypted and tagged; we have a contractual process to exclude ephemeral customer data from multi-day snapshots on Dedicated/Private plans. I will add that exclusion note to the matrix.

2) Audit log retention: default control-plane audit retention is 365 days; for Enterprise customers we offer longer retention as an add-on (configurable up to 7 years) and we can stream audit events to a customer-owned S3 or SIEM on request.
